newsitem.title: ITALY: Defence row, EMU doubts cast shadow at EU party.
newsitem.headline: Defence row, EMU doubts cast shadow at EU party.

text.p: A row over defence and renewed doubt about the fate of Europe's planned single currency cast a shadow on Tuesday over celebrations called to mark 40 years of European integration.

The two issues, both central to the future path of the European Union, intruded in Rome's Renaissance Campidoglio city hall, where EU foreign ministers and European dignitaries gathered to commemorate the bloc's founding Treaty of Rome.
The treaty was signed on March 25, 1957, creating the original six-country European Economic Community (EEC), forerunner of the 15-nation EU.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country currently holds the EU presidency, used the occasion to report to fellow ministers on progress towards a new EU treaty due to be sealed at a summit in Amsterdam in June.

He said progress had been made in a number of fields from foreign policy to judicial affairs but other ministers suggested major work was still needed because of the depth of disagreement among member states.

France, Germany and Italy called for the creation of an EU defence structure with the incorporation of the Western European Union into the bloc but Britain and non-NATO EU states indicated they would have nothing to do with it.
"It is not part of the benefit of the (NATO) Atlantic Alliance to turn the European Union into an organisation for collective security," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said.
In Bonn, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, one of the most tenacious supporters of deeper integration, said the EEC had paved the way for decades of peace, freedom, prosperity and social security.

He coupled his praise with renewed insistence that European economic and monetary union (EMU) should start on time in 1999 on the basis of a rigorous reading of the single currency's guiding Maastricht Treaty.
"We want the euro to come punctually on January 1, 1999. But it is clear this must not be at the expense of monetary stability," he wrote in a newspaper article.
"The stability criteria of the Maastricht Treaty are not open to discussion," Kohl said.

Fresh doubts that countries, including Germany, can meet the tough budget deficit limits needed this year to join the euro were fuelled in Rome by a newspaper interview given by Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.

Dini, whose country is struggling to keep its deficit to within the crucial three percent of Gross Domestic Product, was quoted by business daily Il Sole 24 Ore as saying a one-year delay to the EMU start date would benefit all of Europe.
He insisted his remarks had been misinterpreted, saying an extra year would have been useful but that "Italy is not requesting a delay".
Foreign Ministers Herve de Charette of France and Klaus Kinkel of Germany also dismissed talk of putting EMU back.
"The euro is a question of destiny for Europe, both internally and externally," Kinkel said.

De Charette tied the single currency to the Treaty of Rome, signed by Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany. It went into force in 1958, creating a common market among nations that had fought both the century's world wars.
"The single currency will complete the journey begun in 1958. We are entering into a new period," De Charette said.
